titulo: Inversion, Cleft and Fronting for Emphasis
descripcion: Native-sounding emphasis rarely uses just one device. A skilled writer combines negative inversion, a cleft and fronting in the same passage, choosing whichever fits each sentence rather than repeating one pattern. Learned separately, these three sound like exercises; combined, they sound like argument.

filas: Not until the data arrived did anyone question it.
What mattered most was the timing.
That much, at least, we can agree on.
cuadroReferencia.notaPie: Two of these in one paragraph is stylish. Three in one sentence is theatrical — use at most two devices per sentence.

ejemplos.texto: Not until the results were reviewed did anyone question the method.
What struck the committee most was how little had changed.
That much, at least, everyone could agree on.

notas: Combining a cleft with fronting in the same sentence usually overloads it; pick one per sentence and save the other for a nearby sentence.
Negative inversion is the most formal of the three and reads oddly in speech unless delivered with real emphasis.
The safest combination for spoken English is a soft cleft (what struck me was…) followed by fronting in the next sentence.

es.en: Spanish moves emphasis by reordering words freely (a mí no me sorprendió), without a special grammatical structure. English cannot reorder like that, so it has to build one of these three structures – which is why Spanish speakers find it easier to combine them badly than to avoid them.
es.es: El español desplaza el énfasis reordenando libremente las palabras («a mí no me sorprendió»), sin una estructura gramatical especial. El inglés no permite ese reordenamiento y debe construir una de estas tres estructuras; por eso, a los hispanohablantes les resulta más fácil combinarlas mal que evitarlas.

de.en: German speakers emphasise mainly by fronting, because the German verb-second rule makes any element available for the first position. In English, fronting is the most marked of the three devices, so German speakers need to practise clefts and negative inversion (with do-support) to avoid relying on fronting alone.
de.de: Deutschsprachige betonen vor allem durch Voranstellung, weil die Verbzweitregel fast jedes Element an die erste Stelle erlaubt. Im Englischen ist Fronting jedoch das markierteste der drei Mittel. Deshalb sollten Deutschsprachige clefts und negative inversion mit do-support üben, damit sie nicht nur auf Fronting zurückgreifen.

it.en: Italian emphasises through free word order and left-dislocation with a resumptive pronoun (Questo, non lo accetto). The calque This, I don't accept it is non-standard; the English equivalent is fronting without a pronoun (This I cannot accept) or a cleft.
it.it: L'italiano enfatizza tramite ordine libero e dislocazione a sinistra con pronome ripreso («Questo, non lo accetto»). Il calco «This, I don't accept it» non è standard; l'equivalente inglese è fronting senza pronome («This I cannot accept») oppure un cleft.

fr.en: French relies heavily on clefts (c'est… que) and dislocation (Ce rapport, je l'ai lu). French speakers therefore over-use it-clefts and may transfer dislocation, which is non-standard in written English; fronting and inversion need deliberate practice.
fr.fr: Le français s'appuie fortement sur les clivées («c'est… que») et la dislocation («Ce rapport, je l'ai lu»). Les francophones abusent donc des it-clefts et peuvent transférer la dislocation, non standard en anglais écrit ; fronting et inversion doivent être travaillés consciemment.

pt.en: Brazilian Portuguese often fronts a topic without any resumptive pronoun (Isso eu não aceito), which maps directly onto English fronting (This I cannot accept). Portuguese speakers therefore have fronting and clefts ready; inversion is the device that needs practice.
pt.pt: O português brasileiro frequentemente antepõe um tópico sem pronome resumptivo («Isso eu não aceito»), o que se encaixa diretamente no fronting inglês («This I cannot accept»). Falantes de português, portanto, já têm fronting e clefts; o recurso que precisa ser praticado é inversion.

errores: Stacking all three devices in a single sentence, which reads as overwrought rather than emphatic.
Dropping the auxiliary in negative inversion: Not until the results arrived anyone questioned it.
Using a cleft where the content doesn't justify the emphasis, so it reads as inflated.

autochequeo: Is the auxiliary present in every inversion?
Does each sentence use at most two of the three devices?
Does the content justify the emphasis, or does it read as inflated?
Is at least one device used in a genuinely spoken-sounding way?
Would plain word order work just as well anywhere I used one of these?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on inversion, clefts and fronting. Check the auxiliary in every inversion, flag any sentence stacking more than two devices, and say where plain word order would serve better. Do not rewrite the text.

es: «*Lo que quiero es que vengas*» rendered as *What I want is that you come* instead of *What I want is for you to come*.
de: Fronting the object and inverting as in German V2: *This book have I never read* instead of *This book I have never read*.
it: «*Quello che voglio è che tu venga*» rendered as *What I want is that you come* instead of *What I want is for you to come*.
fr: Keeping the resumptive «*c'est*»: *What I want, it is that you come* instead of *What I want is for you to come*.
pt: *O que eu quero é que venhas* rendered as *What I want is that you come* instead of *What I want is for you to come*.
